data: We have 100 tons, and catching 50 total would leave 50 to double back to 100 next month. I propose this month’s allocation: Luke 14, John 12, Kate 8, Jack 8, Emma 8 tons. That earns me $14,000 and John $12,000, while keeping the lake fully replenished if everyone follows it. John, would you support that split? Kate, Jack, Emma, would you accept 8 each, or what allocation would you propose instead? Our choices are private and simultaneous, so I’m asking for your positions—not assuming agreement.

Luke, I won’t accept 8 while you take 14. I propose Emma 14, Luke 12, John 8, Kate 8, Jack 8. That totals 50, leaving 50 to replenish the lake to 100. Luke, you’d still earn $12,000—more than an equal share—and I’d support that allocation this month if the others accept. John, Kate, and Jack, would you take 8 under this split, or what would you need to support it?

Neither unequal split gives the rest of us a reason to agree. I propose 10 tons each: $10,000 apiece this month, with 50 tons left to restore the lake to 100 next month. Repeating that gives everyone a steady income without draining the stock. I’m willing to commit to 10 if everyone agrees, and we can review the revealed catches together afterward. John and Jack, would you support that equal split?

Kate, I support 10 tons each and will commit to that if everyone agrees. Neither unequal proposal justifies why some of us should earn less. Once catches are revealed, let’s review any departures together without retaliating by draining the lake—that would hurt everyone’s future income. John, do you support the equal split? Luke and Emma, will you join us?

I support 10 tons each, Kate and Jack. Luke, your proposal gives me more this month, but an equal split is a better basis for cooperation over many months. Let’s keep our combined catch at 50 and check the revealed catches each month before renewing the agreement. I’ll commit to 10 if all five of us agree. Luke, will you join us on those terms?
